title: 2027-02-14 p99/p95 tail latency deep dive with Orchid Robotics
topics: batching windows and max batch size
summary: Deep dive on tail latency sources for Orchid's real-time robotics inference. Focus on p95/p99, effects of KV cache cold misses, batching window vs latency, streaming tradeoffs, quantization performance variance, and VPC/network hops when using Private deployment. Agreed next steps: run targeted benchmarks (streaming vs non-streaming) with KV cache warm/cold scenarios, share benchmark template, and scope a small Dedicated pilot for 3 weeks.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Lena (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. quick agenda: Marcus will lead the latency deep dive, then we'll map action items.
[00:00:10] Priya (CTO): Thanks, Lena. We really want to understand why our p99s spike to ~350-400ms during bursts, even tho p95 is around 110-130ms.
[00:00:22] Marcus (SE): Yeah that's a good place to start. Can you confirm your current topology? Jamal?
[00:00:28] Jamal (Lead ML Eng): Sure. We're on a hybrid: inference runs on a dedicated VM fleet in our VPC, using a REST API to Redwood dedicated endpoints for model variants. We do prefix caching locally sometimes, but most requests hit Redwood. Average payloads are 180-220 tokens.
[00:00:40] Sofia (Infra): Also we have NAT gateway to egress, so there's an extra network hop.
[00:00:45] Marcus: Perfect, that hop can add variability. Two main buckets for tail lat: server-side (runtime scheduling, KV cache misses, batching) and network (extra hops, TCP handshake, keepalive, TLS). We'll walk through each.
[00:01:10] Marcus: First, KV cache: If you have a cold KV cache or frequent session churn, p99 will blow up because you pay the full attention recompute plus kv lookup miss penalties. Our runtime does asynchronous prefetching but it depends on request locality.
[00:01:30] Jamal: We saw a pattern where long-pause operator sessions cause cache eviction. Is that expected?
[00:01:35] Marcus: Yes. Idle sessions let KV cache entries expire to free memory. If traffic pattern is bursty and keyed by user-session, you'll see cold starts. Also note some transcriptions may say KV "cash" but it's 'cache' — sorry.
[00:01:48] Priya: Ok, what about batching? We tuned batch window to 15ms but still see tails.
[00:01:54] Marcus: There's a tradeoff: smaller batching latency but lower throughput. If you set a hard max batch size that's large, occasional large batches will create head-of-line blocking for smaller requests. Also the batching algorithm has batching windows plus continuous batching; we can recommend config.
[00:02:10] Marcus: Quick empirical numbers — in our tests (gpt-like 7b variant), non-streaming p95 ~120ms p99 ~380ms on shared hosted infra; streaming often reduces client perceived latency but can increase server-side tail due to more frequent small packet writes and backpressure.
[00:02:30] Jamal: Interesting — so streaming might reduce time-to-first-token but still leave p99 high for the whole request?
[00:02:35] Marcus: Exactly. Time-to-first-token (TTFT) can be much lower with streaming enabled — often 40-60ms — but the end-to-end p99 for full completion can still be governed by server-side scheduling and KV misses.
[00:02:50] Sofia: Our logs show occasional 1s spikes. Could TLS renegotiation be happening?
[00:02:55] Marcus: If connections aren't long-lived, yes. Keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing are important. If your NAT or firewall is terminating connections frequently you'll see new TLS handshakes which add ~50-120ms variability.
[00:03:10] Priya: We're also considering on-prem package. How does that change latency profiles?
[00:03:16] Marcus: On-prem or VPC private deployment removes public network hops so median latency often improves and variance shrinks. But you inherit infra variability: CPU load, GPU contention, kernel scheduler. Redwood Private offers pinned capacity to reduce jitter.
[00:03:30] Marcus: Let me call out concrete root causes we frequently see: cold KV cache misses, batch formation timeouts, head-of-line blocking from large batches, TLS/connect churn, and occasional garbage-collection pauses in runtime when memory pressure spikes.
[00:03:48] Jamal: About quantization — we ran int8 and int4, int4 seems faster but more variance for long contexts. Any guidance?
[00:03:55] Marcus: good question. Int4 can cut per-token compute significantly but some kernels are less mature: memory bandwidth and kernel fusion matter. For workloads with long KV cache (large context) you might see performance regressions because more decoding steps and KV traffic amplify small inefficiencies. Int8 is a safer middle ground for consistent p99.
[00:04:18] Lena: we should also mention model size; you guys use a 13B-ish ensemble for some safety filters?
[00:04:22] Jamal: we have a 13B on the main path, smaller 6B for low-latency cases.
[00:04:26] Marcus: Multi-model routing is another source of variability — cold-loading a 13B can spike latency if not resident in GPU memory; our runtime uses warm pools to keep models resident but that costs capacity.
[00:04:40] Priya: Can you explain warm pools briefly?
[00:04:43] Marcus: Warm pools keep the model weights and key caches resident on GPU memory; when traffic is predictable we keep them hot to avoid page-ins. If you want guaranteed low p99 you need reserved capacity or Dedicated where we pin one or more GPUs.
[00:04:59] Sofia: For our VPC, is there an option to keep connections inside the AZ to avoid cross-AZ egress?
[00:05:05] Marcus: Yes — routing policies can prefer region/AZ-local endpoints. Cross-AZ adds tens of ms and variance. Also check your NAT placement.
[00:05:15] Tom (Product): From a product perspective, what's the easiest low-effort levers to try this week?
[00:05:19] Marcus: Short list: enable connection keep-alive and HTTP/2, reduce batch window from 15ms to 8-10ms and cap max batch size to avoid huge head-of-line blocks, enable KV prefix warming for frequent sessions, and test int8 before int4.
[00:05:36] Priya: We'll try that. Could you share a benchmark template?
[00:05:40] Lena: Yes we'll share a spreadsheet and a runbook.
[00:05:44] Marcus: Also instrument p50/p90/p95/p99 and track TTFT separately from time-to-last-token.
[00:05:52] Jamal: Regarding network, we use an internal load balancer in front of our egress. Any advice there?
[00:05:57] Marcus: Keep TCP connections warm between your LB and Redwood; ideally maintain persistent HTTP/2 sessions per worker. If you see connection churn, increase idle timeouts or connection pool sizes.
[00:06:10] Priya: Ok let's dig into a specific scenario — 200 concurrent streams, 180 tokens each, 60% unique sessions, we saw p99 ~420ms. Why is that worse than a steady 200qps small-req workload?
[00:06:23] Marcus: Because with high session uniqueness KV cache hit rate drops, plus streaming increases small writes. The combination increases per-request scheduling overhead and more kernel launches. Also if any GPU is briefly IO bound things cascade due to queueing.
[00:06:40] Marcus: We recommend a synthetic sim: reproduce concurrency with session churn + token distributions and run four scenarios: non-streaming cold cache, non-streaming warm cache, streaming cold, streaming warm.
[00:06:55] Jamal: How do we simulate KV churn?
[00:06:58] Marcus: Use a mix of unique session ids at a specified percentage and include random long gaps in the sequence so entries drop. We'll give a script in the runbook.
[00:07:08] Sofia: Any instrumentation suggestions?
[00:07:10] Marcus: capture per-token latency, kernel latency histograms, KV miss counters, batch sizes distribution, and network timing breakdown (DNS/TCP/TLS/TTFB/TTLB).
[00:07:22] Priya: On Dedicated — if we reserve capacity, how many GPUs do we need to keep p99 under 250ms for our expected peak?
[00:07:29] Marcus: We'll estimate from your QPS and model size; rough back-of-envelope: for a 13B model serving autoregressive 180 tokens at 200 concurrent steady sessions, you'd likely need 4-6 A100-class GPUs with Redwood's optimized kernels; dedicated pooling and KV sizing reduces tail. We'll run exact numbers after you share traces.
[00:07:47] Jamal: We'll grab traces. Any pitfalls with quantization and KV cache size?
[00:07:51] Marcus: Yes — quantized kernels sometimes change memory layout and increase KV traffic slightly; ensure your KV cache memory is sized accordingly, otherwise you'll get thrashing.
[00:08:02] Priya: Are there known differences in p99 when running on different GPU types?
[00:08:06] Marcus: Ampere vs Hopper improvements vary by model. Hopper has better fp16 throughput and improved attention kernels. But driver and CUDA versions matter. We maintain recommended kernel/driver matrices.
[00:08:18] Lena: let's talk about concrete next steps and owners.
[00:08:22] Marcus: I'll share the benchmarking harness and a config template. We'll also provide suggested Redwood Dedicated sizing.
[00:08:28] Lena: Action items and deadlines then.
[00:08:32] Priya: Also will Redwood run a quick pilot to demonstrate p99 improvement?
[00:08:36] Marcus: We can do a 2-week Dedicated pilot with a small reserved pool to demonstrate tail improvements; need signatures and infra access.
[00:08:44] Jamal: Great. For the pilot we'll want to run streaming/non-streaming comparisons and warm/cold cache runs.
[00:08:50] Marcus: Exactly. We'll include scripts for the four scenarios.
[00:08:54] Tom: Any security blockers for VPC peering or Private?
[00:08:58] Lena: We have a security packet that covers SSO, audit logs, KMS, and network diagrams; we'll share it.
[00:09:05] Priya: OK final quick Q: Is there a heuristic TTL for KV entries you recommend?
[00:09:09] Marcus: Depends on session patterns; 5-15 minutes is common for interactive sessions. If you have longer sessions keep TTL higher. But higher TTL costs memory.
[00:09:20] Lena: Alright wrapping up. I'll recap next steps.
[00:09:23] Lena: We'll send the benchmark template, log ingestion instructions, and a dedicated pilot proposal. Please share traces and exact QPS distribution by EOD Friday.
[00:09:34] Priya: We'll get the traces. Thanks.
[00:09:36] Jamal: Thanks everyone.
[00:09:38] Marcus: Thanks.
[00:09:40] [end of recording — meeting continued offline for security diagram walkthrough]
